title: The Spirit works with the Father and the Son, and speaks as God
english: …inseparability of the Godhead.

He works together with God the Father, who lacks nothing and gives all things, and with his Son, and with them he supplies all things to all, never putting it off until tomorrow. For he is the Spirit of the Father, sharing his knowledge and one with him in mind; his being and his reigning with the Father cannot be taken from him, and he has received as his share the Godhead of the Father, from whom he came forth, subsisting together with him.

And Christ, who holds all authority and all power, did the signs and the wonders and cast out demons with the power of his own most holy Spirit, as the sacred teachers have explained. Micah says: “Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray” (Micah 3:5); and a little later he adds: “For there will be no one who hears them, unless I fill them with strength in the Spirit of the Lord, and of judgment and of might” (Micah 3:7–8). So he said that the Lord works strength in the Spirit of the Lord, to show both the Trinity and the bond of its nature. And he hints at the judgment, in which there is no longer any repentance, and no one who hears. “For in Hades,” he says, “who will confess you?” (Psalm 6:5). And “I will fill them with strength” stands for “I will make a great requital with the divine Spirit.”

Paul, the most approved of the apostles, writes to the Ephesians: “For this reason I bow my knees to God the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner man, so that Christ may dwell in you” (Ephesians 3:14–17); and to the Romans: “I have, then, confidence in Christ Jesus toward God. For I do not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not worked through me, by word and deed, for the obedience of the Gentiles, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15:17–19). Hypostases alike in nature are worthy of like honour. So this saying too comes close to the words “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Matthew reports from the Saviour: “But if I cast out the demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28).

And how he works together with them in enlightenment: it is impossible, then, to be one in accord and in working when the essence is not one. And that is why the Master says at one time, “The Father who dwells in me does the works himself” (John 14:10), and at another, as was just said, “I cast out the demons by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). And that is why Paul too said “in the power of the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15:19), confessing that it was by the divine working of the Trinity that they raised the dead: he himself Eutychus (Acts 20:9–12), and Peter Tabitha (Acts 9:40).
That as God the Father does, so the Holy Spirit too gives revelation, and so is shown to be God and Master.

As God the Father does, so the Holy Spirit too gives revelation, and so is shown to be God and Master, as Luke declares: “There was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel; and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. And he was led by the Spirit into the temple. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he took him up in his arms, and blessed God and said: ‘Now, Master, you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation’” (Luke 2:25–30).

So the Holy Spirit gave the revelation. Simeon took Christ into his arms as the revelation had said. He blessed the one who had revealed it, that is, he glorified the Holy Spirit, having seen the salvation that brought the oracle to its fulfilment. And the very one who had revealed it to him he called God and Master. God the Father also gave revelation, when he declared himself to Job: “Do you think I have answered you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?” (Job 40:8 LXX).

But those who have trained themselves to fight against the true Spirit of God gather from every part of the subject things that belong to other matters and contribute nothing to theology, so as to cast a shadow over the truth. They do not take up precisely what befits the divine mystery and fits the subject, and against this chapter too they bring forward words of Scripture that have no bearing on it. Up and down they repeat, as if it were a great and evident point, that cold and deceitful saying: “From such testimonies,” he says, “the Holy Spirit is brought down to the nature of an angel, since the angels too are seen to give revelation.” And so, out of absurd arguments of their own, they drag the right meanings of Scripture into upheaval. “For it is written,” he says, “in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘Cornelius, a centurion, …

title: The angel learns what the Spirit reveals
english: …a righteous man who fears God, well spoken of by the whole nation of the Jews, received a revelation from a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear words from you’” (Acts 10:22). As for you, if you had kept silent and stitched shut your slandering mouths, you would have done yourselves far more good.

But we refer this chapter too to the more perfect aim; we give good cheer to those who will read it, and we instil a greater zeal for the orthodox faith. So we say that, just as a creature has no communion of nature with the uncreated nature, so neither has it communion in giving revelation. For the angel announces whatever he is moved by the Holy Spirit to say without knowing it himself, and that is why his name is “angel,” that is, messenger. But the Holy Spirit, since he knows all the things of God, as Paul affirms (1 Corinthians 2:10–11), gives revelation in the manner of God, as the Father does: whatever he sees with the sleepless eyes of the Godhead that he wills, and that the Father and the Son will. He does not do it as a servant, as the angel of the guard does. “For the servant does not know what his master is doing” (John 15:15); nor indeed can one of another essence possess the same knowledge as one who is of a different essence. For to each nature belong the knowledge and the memory proper to it; and even what a created nature has come to know sometimes flies away with time.

That is why here too these unfair men have deliberately left out the beginning of the passage in the heat of their argument. For it runs: “While Peter was pondering the matter, the Holy Spirit said to him: ‘Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise, then, and go with them without any doubting, for I have sent them.’ And Peter went down to the men and said: ‘Behold, I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason you have come?’ And they said: ‘Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man’” (Acts 10:19–22), and the rest, as set out above. So, before fair judges, here too the angel is plainly seen to have learned the oracle from the Holy Spirit. For to foretell without error is the distinctive mark of the Godhead; and this is for the good of those who hear, so that, being made secure, they may be saved.

Then do you not see that by bringing in such ideas you somehow begrudge the creation, and find fault, as it were, with him who out of his generosity adorned his own works with the words spoken of himself? For his grace surely goes with such a gift. And by this he in no way dishonoured himself; rather he showed himself worthy of praise, and, as is his custom, made his works shine.

As for us: even though the Holy Spirit’s giving of revelation lends a certain divine majesty to the whole subject, and is enough as testimony when taken by itself, we have still brought forward not that alone, but a whole host of other lofty and indisputable proofs. If you attend to them without hostility, you will surely be more speechless than the fish.

Paul too, then, refutes your plausible trickery most clearly, writing to the Ephesians: “To me, who am less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to bring to light for all what is the plan of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known through the church to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 3:8–10). Consider, then, how far the nature of the angels is removed from knowing anything of the future by itself, and from giving revelation: it learns the great things even through the church of God in this world, which is ourselves. And what he wrote to the Colossians can also help somewhat to persuade on this point. He writes: “This mystery, which was hidden before the ages and from the generations, but has now been revealed to his saints” (Colossians 1:26). For before this, he means, it was known to God alone.

Besides these, there is what Peter declared, as was said before, about the things that brought benefit to all men (I mean the things of the unspeakable plan of salvation), in these words: “Into which,” he says, “angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12). But if they had some innate knowledge, they would not long even to peer into it. Since they do not have it, they fall, in a way, as men do, into an overwhelming desire for things whose knowledge is not within their reach. For it is natural in other matters too that what is easy to find is overlooked, while what is rarer is prized. And yet this too is not by any choice of their own; rather, by the common law of their nature some of them, though I do not say all, are subject to it. “For if,” he says, “God did not spare angels when they sinned” (2 Peter 2:4), what innate knowledge of the …

title: The Spirit reveals as King, the angels as servants; an address to the archangels
english: …things to come, or what sovereign right to give revelation, can they have, as God has? These angels do not know things of themselves, nor do they give revelation by any authority of their own; the fact proves itself even without any argument. If, then, because the one word alone is said of both in common, you have sounded the call to blame and accusation, you have acted rashly and without thought, and not even to the point. For even if some others should happen to say of God the Father that he gives revelation and that he is good, it would not be fitting for us to say the opposite.

Let me tell you something else as well: “Consider whether, by the angel who gave revelation to the centurion, Scripture did not mean the Saviour, the Holy of Holies. For in using this name Scripture appears to speak of him in a hidden way, with great and divine emphasis, because as Son and Word he announced the Father’s will in the plan of salvation. For it did not name him, as it usually does: Michael, Gabriel, or so-and-so.”

What, then, in all our arguments could anyone reasonably charge? And what fault could he find with the faith of the orthodox, which gives no ground anywhere for being called to account? And how is it not right to believe that the Holy Spirit gives revelation royally, that is, as God does, while the angels do so as ministers, that is, as servants? As it is hard, then, as the saying goes, to hold the tiller for one who has no skill in steering, so it is hard also to teach for one to whom the grace of the divine Spirit is not present, the grace that works the salvation of men together with the Father and the Son; for one who does not know the certainty that is found even in the riddles of the sacred oracles, nor the answer given from the understanding of faithful men; and for one whose speech never comes out without a contentious, contradicting and shifting intent.

But I know clearly, O glorious angels of God, who dwell in the heavenly light, that you, being blameless and perfect, were not offended at what I have said about the angels who are like you in nature, though not in the praiseworthiness of their will. Blame has followed them from the beginning, and they seem to you, above all, to be unpersuasive in their struggle against the truth. For my discourse is on behalf of the divine Spirit, who enlightens all things and lavishes on creatures divine gifts that rival those of the Father and his Only-begotten; who sanctified you too, and is glorified by you together with the Father and the Son in the thrice-holy hymn. Better still, you nodded your assent with me when I acclaimed this Spirit of the hypostasis of God as one and only, and as God.

And you would perhaps wish (and in this part my book keeps festival for me), out of the abundance of your goodwill toward the venerable and consubstantial Trinity, that the words spoken from the meaning of the Scriptures by many, and now by me, were your own, that silence might never be laid upon them, and that all men would spend the leisure their affairs leave them on such a subject.

Therefore, for this reason, by the most high judgment, you, holy Michael, were appointed to command the bodiless hosts, and were honoured with a girdle, as it were, of the mind, and you are a kind of fragrance of the all-holy and compassionate Trinity that is Lord of all. And you, holy Gabriel, were chosen to serve the mystery of the plan of salvation that cannot be told, as one who keeps a secret and is faithful. One has been honoured with one God-given gift and another with another, without even asking for it: a gift such as others do not have, and such as we do not have. But we too have a gift such as you do not have.

For God the Word did not become an angel for the sake of the angels who sinned, but a man for the sake of men in sin: without change, without confusion, without sin, beyond telling, as he knows and as he willed, from the Virgin, and in accordance with her flesh and that of all of us; remaining what he was and is and will be, one and the same. “For one,” he says, “is holy, one is Lord, Jesus Christ, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11). And just as he went up from earth into the heavens, so he will come a second time (Acts 1:11), with glorious angelic battalions, myriads upon myriads, serving him; and he will also judge, and act in accordance with his love for mankind.

That is why, after the churches, houses of prayer to God bearing your name, O well-pleasing pair of archangels, have been founded not only in the cities, but also privately in lanes, in houses and in fields, adorned with gold and silver, or even ivory. And people go even to places far from the land that bore them, places that have these houses of prayer set up as, so to speak, halls where prayers are granted. They do not shrink from crossing even a wide sea, if need be, and a road of many days on end …
